analysis.one_liner: Caps out-of-pocket insulin costs at $35 a month for people with private insurance and forces pharmacy middlemen to pass rebates to health plans.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to cap insulin copays at $35 for people with private insurance never received a committee vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The INSULIN Act would have capped what people with private insurance pay out of pocket for insulin at $35 per monthly supply, with no deductible. It would have required pharmacy benefit managers (the middlemen who negotiate drug prices for insurers) to pass 100% of insulin rebates back to health plans, made it harder for brand-name drug companies to use FDA petitions to delay cheaper generic competitors, and sped up approval of biosimilar insulins. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never came up again.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly several million Americans who use insulin and have private insurance would pay no more than $35 for a month's supply, with that amount counting toward their deductible and out-of-pocket maximum. The cap would also have applied to retiree plans and blocked prior-authorization requirements on covered insulin. Faster biosimilar and generic competition could eventually lower prices for everyone.

how_it_helps.text: Beginning in 2024, group and individual health plans must cover selected insulin products with no deductible and cost-sharing capped at $35 per 30-day supply — or 25% of the negotiated price after rebates, whichever is less — starting in 2025 [S2][S3].
The cap would apply across employer plans, marketplace plans, and retiree plans, and cost-sharing payments would count toward deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums [S3].
Plans could not impose prior authorization or other utilization-management hurdles on covered insulin except for clinically justified safety reasons [S3].

Pharmacy benefit managers and insurers would have to remit 100% of insulin-related rebates, fees, and other payments from drug manufacturers back to the health plan, fully disclosed and auditable [S2][S3].

The bill gives the FDA new tools to reject brand-drug makers' petitions filed primarily to delay generic approval and to refer abusive petitions to the Federal Trade Commission, and creates an expedited pathway for biosimilars facing little competition [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name insulin makers would face faster biosimilar competition and a rebate pass-through that exposes the size of the discounts they pay to middlemen. Pharmacy benefit managers would lose a major revenue stream from insulin rebates. Insurers and employers would bear the cost of the $35 cap, which could feed into premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insulin makers, PBMs, and health plans

drawbacks.text: Plans choose which insulin products are 'selected' — they only have to cover at least one of each dosage form and type at the capped price, so newer or more expensive insulins could remain subject to full cost-sharing [S3].
The cap does not apply to insulin dispensed by out-of-network pharmacies, where cost-sharing could still be higher [S3].

The $35 cap shifts costs onto insurers and employer plans, which could pass some of that through in premiums; the bill does not cap the underlying list prices of insulin, only what patients pay at the counter.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections are strong and targeted: a real cap on what insulin users pay, backed by transparency requirements on the middlemen and measures to bring cheaper competitors to market faster. The main design weakness is that plans still pick which insulins get the capped price and can steer patients to cheaper products, but the core protection — $35 for the insulin a plan covers, no deductible — is straightforward and meaningful. The bill never got a chance to be tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee never scheduled a markup or hearing, and the bill died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Jeanne Shaheen introduced the bill on April 25, 2023, co-led with Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine [S1][S3].
Thirteen senators cosponsored it: 7 Republicans, 5 Democrats, and 1 independent [S4].

The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced; the action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no vote [S5].
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, and the bill expired in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, brand-name insulin manufacturers kept their pricing system and pharmacy benefit managers kept their insulin rebate revenue untouched by federal law. Nothing forced the HELP Committee to act on it, so no bloc had to go on record against it.

for.name: Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Joined as co-lead at introduction, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from day one.

against.name: Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill; it sat in committee with no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Democrat-Republican pairing from the start — Shaheen and Collins — and its 13 cosponsors split 7 Republicans, 5 Democrats, and 1 independent, so no party bloc owned or blocked it on the record; it simply never moved.

industries.note: The bill would require PBMs to remit 100% of insulin-related rebates, fees, and discounts from manufacturers back to health plans, fully disclosed and auditable — eliminating a core revenue stream built on the spread between what manufacturers pay and what plans see. PBMs profit from the current rebate system at the expense of plan sponsors and patients.

The bill would not cap list prices directly, but it would expose rebate flows and make it much harder to delay generic and biosimilar competitors through FDA petitions. Insulin makers' current pricing model depends on high list prices negotiated through rebate deals.

The bill creates an expedited FDA pathway for biosimilars facing inadequate competition, speeds facility reinspections, tightens rules on delay petitions, and requires a study of barriers to insulin market entry. Cheaper competing insulins are the business model here, so their gain lines up with cheaper medicine for patients.

Insurers and employer plans bear the cost of the $35 cap and the ban on prior authorization for covered insulin, but they receive the PBM rebate pass-through, which could offset it. Whether they net gain or loss depends on plan design.
